info.title: File Transfer Design Review and Gap Analysis

metadata.displayText: I am continuing the work on this app and this is the design I thought of how the file transfers will work. Can you look through it and all the seams, how it interacts and what it does to see if everything makes sense? Try to find any possible problems/gaps with the design before I start the implementation. Especially go into the details where some things were not said explicitly, try to figure those out if they make sense, to make sure nothing was omitted.

content.text: The user wants me to review a design document for file transfers in their app. Let me start by reading the attached files to understand the design and the app context.

Read file C:\prog\git\YapYap\docs\file\design.md, lines 1-563
1: # File transfer design
2: 
3: This is the design of record for file transfer (v1, 1:1 sends), agreed in the design sessions of November 2026,
4: before implementation. It is the base for implementation; [`../sprints.mmd`](../sprints.mmd) stays authoritative
5: for sprint sequencing at its coarser grain and is not modified by this design.
6: 
7: Related: [`../guide.md`](../guide.md) (layer model, dependency rules, the delivery model in §6),
8: [`../transport.md`](../transport.md) (links, channels, frame limits), [`../router.md`](../router.md) (outbox and
9: relay machinery this design reuses), [`../e2ee.md`](../e2ee.md) (sessions — deliberately **not** used for chunk
10: content, see §4). Diagrams: [`transfer paths.mmd`](transfer%20paths.mmd), [`transfer states.mmd`](transfer%20states.mmd).
11: 
12: ## 1. Scope and philosophy
13: 
14: Two transfer classes, one engine:
15: 
16: - **Small files** — at or below `smallFileMaxBytes` (default 10 MB, the Discord limit; the exact value lives in
17:   config, §15). May traverse relays with store-and-forward. Bounded size, so bounded relay storage.
18: - **Large files** — above the limit, no upper bound (hundreds of GB must work). WebRTC-only: no session means
19:   the transfer waits; bytes never go over Tor and never go to relays.
20: 
21: The core philosophy transplants the guide's delivery model (§6) to files: **the push path (OFFER + chunk flow)
22: is a latency optimization; the pull path (DAG message → REQUEST → serve) is the loss-proof backbone.** A
23: deferred, expired or partial push is never a loss — the message references the file forever, and the receiver
24: can always REQUEST the bytes from a holder.
25: 
26: Grounding facts that shape everything below:
27: 
28: - Chunking is forced everywhere: the WebRTC backend carries at most ~250 KiB per envelope
29:   (`WebRtcBackendConfig.maxPayloadBytes`), Tor at most 4 MB. The chunk size is **derived** (≈220 KiB after
30:   envelope framing) by the composition root, never independently configured (§15).
31: - **No new ARQ is built.** Both transports are reliable per frame (WebRTC data channels are SCTP, configured
32:   ordered + fully reliable; Tor links are framed TCP streams), and the router already gives every envelope
33:   ACK/NACK + dedup + outbox retry. A chunk sent as an ordinary packet is effectively-once per hop. The
34:   SACK-style ACK payload is the **progress/resume** protocol, not loss detection.
35: - Group sends are out of scope for v1, but the design is deliberately encryption-independent: chunk content is
36:   an opaque AEAD blob keyed per file, so group fan-out (sender keys) is additive later without touching the
37:   chunk pipeline.
38: 
39: ## 2. Identity: `fileId` and `transferId`
40: 
41: - **`fileId` = content identity.** Derived from the whole-file hash (`objectHash`), i.e. content addressing.
42:   Stable forever, referenced by the DAG message, and the key for the receiver's chunk tracker, `.part` file,
43:   final file and the permanent attachment store. Free dedup: two senders shipping identical bytes produce the
44:   same `fileId`, and a receiver who already holds it renders the second message instantly from local storage.
45:   The identity *is* the integrity check — no separate `objectHash` field exists anywhere.
46: - **`transferId` = routing session identity.** One push/serve attempt. Keys the relay store, the OFFER, the
47:   outbox marker tag and chunk envelope addressing. Relays never see or need the `fileId`.
48: - The per-file key and the chunking parameters are **bound to `fileId`**, so chunk ciphertext is deterministic:
49:   any holder serving the same `fileId` produces byte-identical chunks. Resume therefore works across transfers
50:   and across serving devices.
51: - Receiver state and `.part` files are `fileId`-scoped (valid across transfers); relay state is
52:   `transferId`-scoped.
53: 
54: ## 3. Wire protocol
55: 
56: All FILE-family envelopes are signed by their author (the `source` field). A relay forwarding stored envelopes
57: replays the original signature verbatim — the relay is never a signature author; the original author's
58: signature plus deterministic ciphertext make replayed content verifiable (§7).
59: 
60: ### 3.1 Message attachments
61: 
62: `MessagePayload.Text` gains an `attachments` list. Each entry is deliberately minimal — everything a receiver
63: needs to render the message and initiate a REQUEST, nothing more:
64: 
65: | Field         | Notes                                            |
66: |---------------|--------------------------------------------------|
67: | `fileId`      | The content hash — also the integrity check      |
68: | `fileName`    | Display                                          |
69: | `mimeType`    | Display / preview                                |
70: | `totalBytes`  | Display and the receiver's expectation           |
71: 
72: Transfer-specific data (chunk parameters, key) arrives only with the OFFER. This is a wire change: codec +
73: round-trip tests, and the attachment bytes are charged against the message size budget (the `Text`
74: `ENCODED_HEADER_RESERVE_BYTES` accounting grows; `wiring/MessageLimits` threads it).
75: 
76: ### 3.2 FileEnvelope payloads (rework of the existing family)
77: 
78: | Kind       | Fields                                                                 | Author / direction                |
79: |------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
80: | `OFFER`    | public half: `chunkSizeBytes`, `totalBytes`, `startIndex`; sealed half: `fileId`, per-file key, `fileName`, `mimeType` | the serving device → target (or relay, for deposits) |
81: | `CHUNK`    | `chunkIndex`, ciphertext                                               | pusher → target (replayed by relay) |
82: | `ACK`      | `fileId`, `highestContiguousChunk`, `missingChunkIndices` (SACK-style)  | target → pusher                    |
83: | `COMPLETE` | `fileId`                                                               | target → original sender           |
84: | `REQUEST`  | `fileId`, held-chunks state (what the requester already holds)         | requester → one candidate device   |
85: | `CANCEL`   | reason                                                                 | sender → relay/target; target → sender (decline) |
86: 
87: Notes on the rework:
88: 
89: - The existing `FileChunk`/`FileControlPayload`/`FileTransferClass`/`FileTransportPreference` wire types are
90:   dropped. The small/large distinction is a sender-engine policy driven by the config threshold, not wire
91:   state; transport preference is path policy (§5), not a negotiated field. `maxInFlightChunks` is engine
92:   config (§15), not wire.
93: - `CHUNK` loses its `chunkCount` — the covered set is defined by the OFFER (§3.4).
94: - The existing per-chunk hash idea stays dead: AEAD tags detect corruption at decrypt; whole-file integrity is
95:   the `fileId` itself.
96: 
97: ### 3.3 The OFFER's two halves
98: 
99: - **Public half** — what relays need for their storage contract: `chunkSizeBytes`, `totalBytes`, `startIndex`.
100:   From these the relay derives the file-level chunk count (`ceil(totalBytes / chunkSizeBytes)`) and the covered
101:   suffix (§3.4). The `transferId` rides the envelope header.
102: - **Sealed half** — `fileId`, the per-file key, display metadata; sealed to the target device. Relays can never
103:   read it, and never learn the `fileId` (two transfers of the same file are not correlatable at a relay).
104: 
105: The receiver derives its completeness oracle — the file-level chunk count — from **any** OFFER, even a partial
106: one. This matters for bare transfers (no DAG message, §10) whose only OFFER may be a remainder deposit.
107: 
108: Key transport, restated: the per-file key travels **raw inside the message plaintext** (the message path already
109: E2EEs per device) and **sealed to the addressee inside the OFFER**. The receiver stores the key from whichever
110: carrier arrives first.
111: 
112: ### 3.4 Covered sets are always suffixes
113: 
114: Every transfer covers a **contiguous suffix** of the file's chunk sequence: `[startIndex, fileCount-1]`.
115: 
116: - Initial full transfer: `startIndex = 0`.
117: - Direct-link break remainder: `startIndex = highestContiguousAckedPrefix + 1` (§6.4).
118: - REQUEST serve: `startIndex = lowest index the requester is missing` (a few re-sent duplicates are harmless —
119:   the receiver dedups).
120: - Large-path resume: the checkpoint is a contiguous prefix, so resumption is a suffix by construction.
121: 
122: This invariant is what keeps the OFFER to a single start index (no lists, no bitmaps) and collapses the sending
123: engine's per-depot bookkeeping to one number per depot: its resume point.
124: 
125: ## 4. Crypto
126: 
127: - **Per-file symmetric key** (AEAD, e.g. ChaCha20-Poly1305), created at send time, bound to the `fileId`.
128:   Chunk content **never** goes through the Double Ratchet: a long file would explode ratchet state, `MAX_SKIP`
129:   bounds out-of-order tolerance, and one lost chunk would break the chain for interleaved messages.
130: - **Deterministic ciphertext**: nonce derived from (`fileId`, `chunkIndex`). This is load-bearing — it makes
131:   the relay's stored bytes identical to any holder's, so the receiver's `(fileId, chunkIndex)` dedup and resume
132:   work across all sources.
133: - WebRTC's DTLS already encrypts the channel; the app-layer AEAD is kept regardless — negligible cost
134:   (AEAD is GB/s), uniform format across paths, determinism across holders, and independence from
135:   transport-stack correctness.
136: - New `FileProtection` implementation (sealing, signing, per-chunk AEAD via `CryptoProvider`) replaces the
137:   `PlaintextFileProtection` placeholder.
138: 
139: ## 5. Path selection
140: 
141: **Small files** mirror the message model exactly: direct over any open link first; relay deposit only when the
142: direct path looks doubtful. The deposit triggers are the existing `RelayBackup` triggers (no link at claim
143: time, retry, no ACK in time) **plus** a chunk-level stall trigger (§6.3). The trigger *policy* is extracted into
144: a shared component that messages and files both consult; payload construction stays per-path.
145: 
146: **Relay choice is `RelaySelectionPolicy`'s, unchanged from messages.** It returns whichever relays its
147: reliability math picks for the target (targeting `relayTargetSuccessProbability`, floor `minRelayScore`), and
148: the number it returns varies up to the `maxRelays` cap. The deposit does not choose a count — it offers the
149: covered set to **every relay the policy returns**. An empty selection means no deposit; the pull path covers
150: it.
151: 
152: **Large files**: OFFER and chunks are both **WebRTC-only**. The large path therefore never touches the outbox:
153: the engine holds its IN_FLIGHT state, subscribes to session events, and sends directly when a session exists
154: (no per-entry transport mask is needed in v1). The receiver learns "a big file is pending" from the DAG
155: message, which does travel over Tor/relays — that is the "waiting for session" UX.
156: 
157: ## 6. The push machinery (routing layer)
158: 
159: One mechanism, two chunk sources. The **pusher** owns: the OFFER-as-marker lifecycle, chunk outbox rows, the
160: in-flight window, the stall detector, deposit-on-stall, and resume. It speaks pure router vocabulary (packets,
161: outbox, ACKs, links), so it lives in **routing**, parameterized by a ciphertext source:
162: 
163: - **Sender's push** — source implemented by the orchestrator (reads the app-internal file, AEAD-encrypts on
164:   the fly) through a `FileChunkSource` port the router declares.
165: - **Relay's forward** — source implemented by routing itself (reads the `file_relay_chunks` store). The relay
166:   is simply another sender whose "file" is a DB table (§7).
167: 
168: ### 6.1 The marker
169: 
170: The OFFER is enqueued as a normal outbox entry with `OutboxTag.Kind.FILE`, id = `transferId`, and standard
171: semantics — the delivery contract's "ACK = processed" is untouched:
172: 
173: - ACK (the offer was accepted) → marker removed; **the engine owns everything after**.
174: - Terminal NACK (DECLINED: relay full, target declined) → marker removed; the engine tries the next relay or
175:   re-offers later.
176: - Expiry → marker removed; the engine re-arms from its own state.
177: 
178: The envelope's `expiresAt` carries the file-scale TTL (`fileTransferTtl`) — the outbox honors it natively via
179: its expiry prune. Claim/lease semantics on the engine side ensure an offer **retry resumes rather than
180: restarts** an active flow.
181: 
182: The marker is establishment-only. It is never held open until completion: that would need a "processed but
183: don't ACK yet" inbound result, fight every message-scale outbox assumption, and duplicate state the engine
184: already owns (see §17, rejected alternatives).
185: 
186: ### 6.2 The chunk phase (small path)
187: 
188: Chunks are individual outbox rows (tagged FILE, id = `transferId`) — per-chunk retry, dedup and restart
189: survival come free. A window (`maxInFlightChunks`) bounds pending rows: each row holds a ~220 KiB blob, so a
190: window of 16 ≈ 3.5 MB of outbox per transfer. The existing `outboxMaxInFlightPerTarget` already bounds dispatch
191: concurrency; if chunk throughput ever needs more, a per-tag-kind cap override is the knob (deferred, §18).
192: 
193: Outbox extensions required: the new tag kind, and `packetId` on `OutboxOutcome` so the engine maps a chunk
194: outcome to its index. Unacked chunks are exactly the tagged rows still queued, so the engine's pending set is
195: reconstructable from the outbox — no parallel per-chunk table on the send side. The per-chunk **plan**
196: (offsets, §10) is `fileId`-bound and pre-materialized only for small files.
197: 
198: ### 6.3 Stall detection
199: 
200: No chunk ACK within `chunkAckTimeout` (30–60 s) → the transfer is flagged stalled → small path: deposit the
201: remainder to relays at once (§6.4); large path: pause and await session re-establishment.
202: 
203: Deposit-on-stall is **insurance, not restart-survival**: the DB state (transfer rows, plan, outbox rows)
204: resumes on boot regardless. What the deposit buys is that the already-pushed prefix never again needs the
205: sender and the target online simultaneously.
206: 
207: ### 6.4 Deposit rules: one jump, parallel redundancy
208: 
209: - **The direct link breaks or stalls → deposit the remainder.** The remainder is the suffix after the
210:   **highest contiguous ACKed prefix** (`startIndex = prefix + 1`). This is safe by construction: any ACK holes
211:   below the prefix end are inside the remainder by definition, so the simplification never excludes a hole; it
212:   may re-send a few chunks the target already got, which the receiver dedups.
213: - **Parallel redundancy, never sequential.** The covered set goes, identical, to every relay
214:   `RelaySelectionPolicy` returns (§5). If one relay's deposit stalls, that is the outbox's business — per-chunk
215:   rows retry at their own cadence, and the reservation TTL eventually cleans what never lands. **The sender
216:   never chases a failing relay by re-depositing its missing parts elsewhere.**
217: - **One jump, ever.** Combined with the no-chaining rule for forwarding relays (§7), file ciphertext makes at
218:   most one relay hop: sender → relay → target. No relay-to-relay spread.
219: - If every deposit and the direct path all die, the pull path (§9) is the backstop — that is its job.
220: 
221: ### 6.5 Completion and teardown
222: 
223: Each relay deposit is an **independent transfer** that runs until *that relay* holds its full covered set, or
224: TTL. One relay completing never cancels the others — the whole point of multiple deposits is the reliability
225: probability math behind `RelaySelectionPolicy`.
226: 
227: The send's push phase ends when **every deposit has resolved** (complete at its relay, or expired), or earlier
228: on the only two legitimate cross-deposit teardowns:
229: 
230: - **Target-confirmed full receipt**: the target's SACK-style progress ACKs are ordinary routable packets
231:   (target → sender via its own outbox, direct or relayed — the same store-and-forward as anything else), so
232:   "the target has everything" reaches the sender even when only relays delivered. On that signal the engine
233:   politely CANCELs outstanding deposits so relays free quota immediately.
234: - **User cancel**: CANCEL to every active transfer and deposit.
235: 
236: `COMPLETE` (target → original sender) is the explicit form of the first signal.
237: 
238: ## 7. The relay
239: 
240: The relay is **dumb to content, smart about its storage contract**. It cannot read chunks (no key), cannot
241: verify content (the `fileId` hash is over plaintext — count-based wholeness is the ceiling, by design, and
242: nothing smarter helps any actor), and never learns the `fileId`. It is not a REQUEST candidate (§9). Its
243: storage is DB tables, not a files directory — transactional admission, eviction and crash recovery for free at
244: ≤10 MB per transfer.
245: 
246: ### 7.1 Signature verification at the door
247: 
248: The relay verifies the **original sender's signature** on the OFFER and on every CHUNK before storing (the
249: inner `FileEnvelope.source` must be a known, non-banned device; its public key comes from the identity views
250: routing may read). Without this, anyone who learns a `transferId` could stuff junk chunks into the store: they
251: would fail the target's decrypt later, but they would poison wholeness counting and waste quota. Verified
252: envelopes only; unverified are dropped.
253: 
254: ### 7.2 Lifecycle
255: 
256: 1. **Admission**: the OFFER's public half is checked against `relayFileBudgetBytes`; the covered suffix's
257:    bytes are reserved, or the OFFER is NACKed DECLINED (the existing vocabulary). The relay also stores the
258:    OFFER's payload blob verbatim — the forward re-uses it without re-signing (§7.4).
259: 2. **Hold**: chunks land in `file_relay_chunks`, PK (`transferId`, `chunkIndex`) — dedup is free, and
260:    re-deposits after a stall no-op.
261: 3. **Wholeness gate**: every index of the covered suffix present → the transfer is *whole*. **Incomplete
262:    transfers are never pushed and never offered**: the relay stays silent, and the **reservation TTL** (idle
263:    expiry) cleans up what the sender never finished. The TTL is load-bearing for budget correctness, not
264:    hygiene.
265: 4. **Forward = the same pusher, DB source**: once whole, the stored OFFER payload is enqueued to the target as
266:    a normal outbox marker; ACK → chunk rows stream from the store; per-chunk ACKs from the target delete rows;
267:    the transfer row is dropped when drained.
268:    - Outer `BinaryEnvelope.source` = the relay, inner `FileEnvelope.source` = the original sender with its
269:      signature intact — exactly the message-transit pattern (`MessageInboundHandler`): relay transit is
270:      unauthenticated at the outer layer, content is authenticated inside.
271:    - **Blind full-send in v1**: the target ACKs every chunk it processes; a chunk it already holds (another
272:      relay, or the direct path) returns Success → row deleted. Duplicate waste is bounded; an OFFER-response
273:      carrying held-state is a later optimization, not a correctness need (§18).
274:    - **No chaining**: a forwarding relay never deposits its forwarded transfer at other relays. Stall at a
275:      forwarding relay = park and wait (outbox-native).
276: 5. **Eviction**: whole-transfer LRU over `file_relay_transfers` — never a single row (evicting chunk 37 of 46
277:    silently kills the transfer).
278: 6. **Forget after delivery** — same as relayed messages: rows die as the target ACKs, the transfer row dies
279:    when drained.
280: 
281: **Invariant**: *anything a relay pushes is whole.* A forwarded push that stalls is therefore always a link
282: problem (the forwarder retries from its complete store), never a content problem — the receiver needs no stall
283: detection on relay pushes.
284: 
285: **Restart recovery is free**: the forward's state is entirely outbox rows + store rows, both in the DB, both
286: already recovered by boot; wholeness is recomputed from the store.
287: 
288: ## 8. The receiver
289: 
290: - An OFFER (or the DAG message) creates a `fileId`-scoped tracker row. The key arrives sealed in the OFFER or
291:   raw in the message; the receiver stores it from whichever lands first. Transfers merge into one tracker —
292:   the receiver is transfer-agnostic.
293: - **Reserve** `<fileId>.part` at `totalBytes` with an **explicit free-space check** (preallocation is sparse
294:   on most filesystems — stat the volume, not the file). Insufficient space or a user decline → a DECLINED
295:   response and a clean failure; mid-write ENOSPC fails the transfer cleanly. Auto-accept below a size
296:   threshold, ask above it (a config knob).
297: - Chunks: verify signature → decrypt (AEAD) → dedup by (`fileId`, `chunkIndex`) — **duplicates are normal
298:   traffic** (multiple relay deposits plus the direct path all deliver overlapping sets) → hand to the writer.
299: - **Small path**: out-of-order chunks go through a bounded in-memory reorder buffer (worst case the file cap,
300:   ≤10 MB; usually near-zero); the contiguous prefix drains to the `.part` as it advances. Per-chunk tracker
301:   rows (≤ ~46) record the received set.
302: - **Large path**: the channel is ordered + reliable, so chunks arrive in order — pure sequential append plus a
303:   bytes-written **checkpoint**; no per-chunk rows (a 100 GB file would otherwise be ~476k rows).
304: - All chunks present (file-level count from the OFFER/message) → **verify the hash (`fileId`) → atomic rename
305:   → status READY**. Never READY without verification.
306: - Progress ACKs (SACK-style, `fileId`-scoped merged state) flow back to the pusher; each pusher interprets
307:   them against its covered suffix.
308: 
309: ## 9. The pull path: REQUEST
310: 
311: The recovery mechanism for everything the push path failed to deliver, and the only way history-acquired
312: files get their bytes.
313: 
314: - **Trigger** (orchestrator inbound pipeline, during DAG processing): a message references a `fileId` with no
315:   completed local file and no active transfer. Guards:
316:   - not while a transfer is IN_FLIGHT for that `fileId` (the OFFER may simply be behind the message in
317:     flight);
318:   - terminal states distinguish **re-requestable** (`EXPIRED`) from **refused** (`DECLINED`/`CANCELLED` —
319:     never auto-resurrect a file the user declined);
320:   - dedup by `fileId` (message duplicates create one row);
321:   - a grace period before the first attempt (the `firstAttemptAt` pattern — the receiver cannot know an OFFER
322:     is still pending sender-side).
323: - **One candidate at a time, never parallel** — parallel asks would make N devices each serve the entire file;
324:   that is the spam/DDoS shape. Candidates: the sender's devices, then own-account siblings (room members
325:   later), link-availability filtered like sync. An attempt covers the **handshake only** (REQUEST → OFFER or
326:   DECLINED); the transfer that follows has its own lifecycle. DECLINED rules a device out; expiry demotes it;
327:   the next candidate is asked at once.
328: - The candidate-asking loop is **extracted as a shared core with `SyncRetryProcessor`** (the needs now
329:   coincide; on success the file request hands off to the transfer engine instead of consuming a reply payload
330:   — a callback seam, not a structural fork).
331: - The REQUEST carries held-chunks state; the serving device (any holder: original sender, sibling that
332:   completed) re-runs the push engine with a **fresh `transferId`** for the same `fileId`, serving the suffix
333:   from the lowest missing index — deterministic ciphertext makes the bytes identical, so resume is exact.
334: - All candidates declined/expired → "file unavailable" (terminal, but a new sync or re-open can retry).
335: - Relays are **not** candidates: they are transient push caches with forget-after-delivery semantics; pulling
336:   from them was simplified away.
337: 
338: ## 10. Storage and retention
339: 
340: - **Sender/holder**: the GUI copies a file into **app-internal storage** before sending. This makes the chunk
341:   source immutable across restarts (resume cannot fail because the user moved the original), is the render
342:   source for the conversation, and is the re-serve source for REQUESTs. **Keep forever** is the default
343:   policy — serverlessness forces it (the bytes are on a device or nowhere; there is no lazy-loading when a
344:   user scrolls back a year). Knob: per-account quota with LRU above it.
345: - **Receiver**: the same permanent store once READY; `.part` until verified.
346: - **Relay**: transient ciphertext only — budget-capped, TTL'd, forget-after-delivery.
347: - **Bare transfers** (no message ever) are a named limitation: they are forgotten when both sides forget
348:   them. Anything referenced by a message is recoverable forever via REQUEST.
349: 
350: ## 11. File I/O: pure kotlinx.io
351: 
352: kotlinx.io is the house standard already (`ConfigStore`, `JvmAppLogger`, `KmpTorBackend`, `DataDirLock`,
353: `Platform`), and v1 uses **only** it — positioned I/O is on kotlinx.io's roadmap (files-API redesign,
354: kotlinx-io issue #241) but not shipped, so the design avoids needing it:
355: 
356: - **Large path, both sides, fully sequential**: the sender reads linearly via `source()` and **keeps the
357:   source open across session drops** (a drop needs no reopen); the receiver appends via `sink(append = true)`
358:   — append position *is* the checkpoint, no seeking; verification reads linearly.
359: - **Small-path receiver**: the in-memory reorder buffer (§8) replaces positioned writes.
360: - **Sender re-reads**: open + linear skip — trivial at ≤10 MB; for a large file the skip to the checkpoint is
361:   paid only on a **full app restart mid-transfer** (a one-time bounded read of the already-sent prefix).
362: - The chunk-shaped I/O boundary (`readChunk`/`writeChunk`-style module) still exists as a module, with a
363:   kotlinx.io-only implementation inside — so when #241 ships positioned read/write, the swap is internal, not
364:   a design change.
365: 
366: ## 12. Layering and data ownership
367: 
368: **Two state homes by role, one shared machinery:**
369: 
370: - `file_transfers` and friends (orchestrator) model **only own traffic**: our sends, receives and
371:   serves-on-REQUEST. A file we relay for someone else never gets a row there.
372: - Foreign traffic state lives entirely in routing: `file_relay_*` plus the outbox rows of the forward. The
373:   relay's forward is driven by routing's own pusher reading routing's own store.
374: - The shared piece is the pusher (§6), which lives in routing because it speaks packet vocabulary.
375: 
376: The precedent is already in the codebase: the router stores and forwards foreign *messages* purely in routing
377: tables (`outbox` `is_relay` rows, `dedup`) and the orchestrator never sees them. Files follow that line — so a
378: headless relay node's orchestrator (file service, REQUEST logic, GUI progress) is completely uninvolved in
379: forwarding. Serve-on-REQUEST is the one relay-node case that *is* orchestrator business (we hold the file →
380: own traffic → our `file_transfers` row with the stored descriptor and key, pushed through the same machinery).

382: ### Module layout
383: 
384: | Layer      | Owns                                                                                        |
385: |------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
386: | `protocol` | `FileEnvelope` rework (§3.2), `Text.attachments` (§3.1), codecs + round-trip tests           |

393: The large-path transfer session (offer → accept/reject → active → ended/failed) is designed as a sibling of
394: the AV session contract, so the planned shared session machinery ("offer retry queues for voice and file",
395: sprints s6a) plugs in rather than forks.

397: ### Large-path transport detail
398: 
399: A per-**transfer dedicated data channel** (labeled, opened on the existing peer connection — no renegotiation)
400: carries the stream. This also solves head-of-line blocking: multiplexing a 100 GB stream onto the single
401: ordered envelope channel would starve messages and ACKs behind file data. Pacing is the channel's own flow
402: control (`bufferedAmount` / low-threshold backpressure), which **replaces the app-level window for this path**.

440: ## 14. State machines
441: 
442: See [`transfer states.mmd`](transfer%20states.mmd). Compact listing:
443: 
444: - **Sender transfer**: CREATED → IN_FLIGHT (offer accepted) → COMPLETED / EXPIRED / CANCELLED. A large
445:   transfer's IN_FLIGHT includes waiting for a session (engine loop detail, not a distinct status).
446: - **Receiver (`fileId`-scoped)**: PENDING → IN_FLIGHT (`.part` reserved, key stored) → VERIFYING (file-level
447:   count met) → READY (hash verified, renamed) / FAILED / DECLINED. IN_FLIGHT that never progresses expires →
448:   the REQUEST trigger re-opens.
449: - **Relay transfer**: RESERVED (admitted) → WHOLE (covered suffix complete) → FORWARDING (offer acked) →
450:   DRAINED; EXPIRED (reservation TTL or transfer TTL) from RESERVED/WHOLE.
451: - **Request**: PENDING → ASKING (one candidate) → SATISFIED (OFFER received; the serve transfer takes over) /
452:   UNAVAILABLE (every candidate declined or expired); ASKING → PENDING on timeout/non-terminal NACK with the
453:   next candidate.
454: - **Marker** (outbox row): QUEUED → dispatched → gone on ACK / terminal NACK / expiry; retries resume, never
455:   restart.
456:

458: 
459: Per guide §2, each layer's config type lives next to its code:
460: 
461: - `FileServiceConfig` (orchestrator, `runtime/file`): `smallFileMaxBytes = 10 MB`, `maxInFlightChunks`,
462:   receive directory, retention quota, auto-accept threshold.
463: - `RouterConfig` additions: `relayFileBudgetBytes`, `fileTransferTtl` (days — marker, relay reservation and
464:   transfer lifetimes), `chunkAckTimeout`, `fileRequestAttemptTimeout`, `fileRequestFirstAttemptDelay` (the
465:   grace period).
466: - Derived in wiring (`FileLimits`, chained from the transport backend configs like `MessageLimits`):
467:   `chunkSizeBytes ≈ 220 KiB`.
468: - Reused unchanged: `RelaySelectionPolicy` with `relayTargetSuccessProbability`, `minRelayScore` and the
469:   `maxRelays` cap (§5); the outbox's own retry/park/expiry behavior.
470: 
471: ## 16. Invariants
472: 
473: 1. Anything a relay pushes is whole — count-based check over the covered suffix; this is the ceiling by
474:    design (the relay cannot and must not verify content).
475: 2. One relay hop, ever: deposit-to-relays happens only at the original sender, redundancy is parallel (same
476:    covered set at every policy-selected relay), forwarding relays never re-deposit, the sender never chases a
477:    failing relay.
478: 3. Relays are not REQUEST candidates; relays forget after delivery.
479: 4. Never READY without all chunks and hash verification.
480: 5. The per-file key travels raw only inside message E2EE plaintext; sealed everywhere else.
481: 6. Deterministic ciphertext: key per `fileId`, nonce per (`fileId`, `chunkIndex`); chunking parameters are
482:    `fileId`-bound.
483: 7. Covered sets are contiguous suffixes; per-depot engine state is one resume point.
484: 8. The marker is establishment-only; ACK = processed (the §6 delivery contract is untouched); the engine owns
485:    everything after.
486: 9. Receiver state is `fileId`-scoped (transfer-agnostic); relay state is `transferId`-scoped.
487: 10. One REQUEST candidate at a time.
488: 11. Terminal states distinguish re-requestable (`EXPIRED`) from refused (`DECLINED`/`CANCELLED`).
489: 12. The relay verifies the original sender's signature on OFFER and CHUNK before storing anything.
490: 13. Bare transfers (no message) are forgettable when both sides forget them — a named limitation.
491: 
492: ## 17. Rejected alternatives
493: 
494: Recorded so they are not relitigated:
495: 
496: - **Whole file as one packet** — transport frame caps (250 KiB WebRTC, 4 MB Tor) make it impossible; chunking
497:   everywhere.
498: - **Chunk content through the Double Ratchet** — ratchet state explosion, `MAX_SKIP` bounds, chain breakage
499:   for interleaved messages; per-file symmetric key instead.
500: - **Relay-held chunks as outbox `is_relay` rows** — the relay cache budget is shared with messages (one 10 MB
501:   file would consume it entirely), per-row LRU eviction strands transfers, and making it safe would push
502:   transfer-awareness into the most battle-tested component. Dedicated tables isolate it.
503: - **Relay chunks on disk** — at ≤10 MB the DB gives transactional admission/eviction/crash recovery for free.
504: - **Marker held open until transfer completion** — needs a "processed but don't ACK" result, fights every
505:   message-scale outbox assumption, and duplicates state the engine owns.
506: - **Parallel REQUEST fan-out** — N devices each serving the entire file is the spam shape; one candidate at a
507:   time.
508: - **Relays as REQUEST candidates** — simplified away; relays are pure push caches.
509: - **Eager per-chunk relay forwarding** — gate on wholeness instead: the latency cost is theoretical (the relay
510:   path is only used when the direct path already failed), and the invariant "a relay push is always whole" is
511:   worth more.
512: - **Sparse covered sets** — the suffix invariant (§3.4) covers every case with bounded duplicate re-sends and
513:   one number of per-depot state.
514: - **Sequential relay re-deposit (chasing)** — spreads the file across the network; one jump.
515: - **Media tracks (RTP/SRTP) for file streaming** — real-time and lossy by design; files need the data
516:   channel's reliability.
517: - **Plaintext streaming over DTLS without app-layer AEAD** — kept for determinism across holders, uniformity
518:   with the relay path, and transport independence.
519: - **Positioned-I/O platform port in v1** — pure kotlinx.io with a reorder buffer and open+skip instead; swap
520:   in kotlinx.io positioned I/O when it ships (#241).
521: 
522: ## 18. Deferred
523: 
524: Group sender keys (additive by design); OFFER-response carrying held-state (bandwidth optimization for
525: duplicate relay forwards); per-tag-kind outbox in-flight cap; relays as REQUEST candidates (rejected for v1);
526: disk-based relay store (only if `smallFileMaxBytes` grows); positioned I/O via kotlinx.io #241; GUI-API
527: contract for the send/progress/decline surface (to be written with the GUI work).
528: 
529: ## 19. Test matrix
530: 
531: - Small file, target offline: deposit → wholeness → forward on surfacing → verify → READY.
532: - Mid-transfer restarts: sender restart mid-push (resumes from plan/outbox); relay restart mid-forward (free
533:   recovery); receiver restart mid-assembly (tracker + reorder).
534: - Direct-link break mid-send: remainder deposit at the policy-selected relays; holes below the prefix are
535:   inside the remainder; target completes from direct prefix + relay remainder.
536: - Duplicate relay forwards: target dedups (`fileId`, `chunkIndex`); second relay drains on already-held ACKs.
537: - Stall → immediate deposit; sender killed right after → relays hold a whole copy.
538: - Eviction pressure → DECLINED at admission → engine tries the next relay / re-offers later.
539: - Sender dies mid-deposit: partial never pushed; reservation TTL cleans; target's REQUEST recovers from a
540:   holder.
541: - Large file: no session → waits (never Tor); session opens → streams; session drops → checkpoint resume;
542:   restart mid-transfer → linear-skip resume.
543: - History sync on a fresh device: attachment renders from the message, REQUEST pulls the bytes with exact
544:   resume from held-state.
545: - Declined / cancelled / no-space / ENOSPC paths; "file unavailable" after all candidates decline.
546: - No-chaining negative test: a forwarding relay must never deposit elsewhere.
547: - Unverified chunk injection at a relay (bad signature) is dropped and never counts toward wholeness.
548: - Bare transfer send/receive without any DAG message.

1: # YapYap Backend Guide
2: 
3: This guide explains what YapYap is, how the core is layered, and the rules new code must follow. It describes
4: the design, not the current state of any one class: when the code and this guide disagree, treat that as a bug
5: in one of them and raise it, don't silently follow the code.
6: 
7: Deeper references: [`transport.md`](transport.md) (Tor/WebRTC links), [`router.md`](router.md) (router
8: internals), [`e2ee.md`](e2ee.md) (sessions and ratchets), [`file/design.md`](file/design.md) (file transfer
9: design, pre-implementation), [`global events.md`](global%20events.md) (accounts,
10: devices, admin chain), [`room events.md`](room%20events.md) (rooms and membership), [`gui-api.md`](gui-api.md)
11: (what the GUI may use).
12: 
13: ## 1. What YapYap is
14: 
15: - A messenger for a small trusted network (about 10–20 users). Correctness, resilience and maintainability win
16:   over scale.
17: - No servers it depends on. Every device runs the Kotlin core as a library; the same core runs headless on
18:   optional always-on nodes (e.g. a Raspberry Pi) that act as relays and availability anchors.
19: - Traffic:
20:     - text and small images over Tor, with store-and-forward through relays when the recipient is offline;
21:     - a direct low-latency path over WebRTC when both sides are online;
22:     - large files and audio/video over WebRTC peer-to-peer, signaled over Tor.
23: - The GUI is Compose Multiplatform. The frontend is ordinary messenger UI; the backend is where the novel work
24:   is, and it is what this guide is about.
25: 
26: ## 2. The layer model
27: 
28: The core is layered like a small network stack, not like a three-tier app. Three layers carry traffic, top to
29: bottom, and a few services sit beside them.
30: 
31: ```
32:   GUI ──► Orchestrator   accounts, rooms, messages, history (DAG), folds, onboarding, sync
33:               │  AccountId + payloads
34:               ▼
35:           Router         devices, envelopes, outbox, ACK/NACK, dedup, links, relays, pings
36:               │  PeerId / TorEndpoint + BinaryEnvelope
37:               ▼
38:           Transports     Tor streams, WebRTC data channels: bytes in, bytes out
39: 
40:   Beside them:  protocol (wire types + codecs) · crypto (keys, E2EE) · protection (envelope sign/encrypt)
41:                 storage (SQLDelight, keyring) · config · logging
42:   Built by:     the composition root (wiring)
43: ```
44: 
45: A three-layer split (presentation / business / data) would merge the router and the transports into "data" and
46: lose the boundary that matters most here: who knows about devices and packets, and who doesn't.
47: 
48: ### Orchestrator — "what is said, and to whom"
49: 
50: - Speaks **accounts, rooms and payloads**: `AccountId`, `RoomId`, `MessagePayload`, `BootstrapPayload`, global
51:   and room events.
52: - Owns the message history (the DAG), the global and room folds, onboarding and recovery, typing state, and **sync**
53:   (working out what is missing, serving sync requests, retrying them).
54: - Hands a payload to the router addressed to an account and gets back an account-level report. Its own onion
55:   endpoint (for invites and its own AddDevice) comes from `Router.localTorEndpoint()`; the roster's "last seen"
56:   comes from `Router.accountReach()`, per account and for display only. Other devices' endpoints in the roster are
57:   the ones they declared on the chain.
58: - Models devices only as **members of an account**: an `Account` carries its `AccountDevice`s, which hold
59:   identity facts (keys, type, status, provisional, declared endpoint) and nothing the router learned about reaching
60:   them. It may name a device as the
61:   *subject* of an identity fact (add/remove a device, re-verify messages from a device) using `PeerId`, but **never
62:   addresses** one. The single exception is bootstrap: before an account exists, an
63:   intro or recovery request is sent to a device id plus an out-of-band `TorEndpoint`.
64: - Fans out per room; the router fans out per account. Whoever authors a room or global event reads the room's
65:   members after the fold commits, so a just-added member is included and a removed one is not.
66: - Never sees `BinaryEnvelope`, packet ids, link or session state, transport types, or Tor types.
67: 
68: ### Router — "get this payload there"
69: 
70: - Speaks **devices and envelopes**: `PeerId`, `BinaryEnvelope`, packet ids.
71: - Fans a payload out to every device of the target account, protects it (via protection), queues it in the
72:   outbox, picks a link, retries, deposits relay copies, and handles ACK/NACK and dedup.
73: - Keeps links alive, sends pings, tracks peer availability, and exposes presence to the orchestrator **per
74:   account only** (`onlineAccounts`); which device carries an account stays inside the router.
75: - Reads accounts and devices through `DeviceDirectory` (account → devices, status, the endpoint a device
76:   declared), a read-only view it declares, and who it is through crypto's `LocalIdentity`. What it learns about
77:   reaching peers (proven endpoints, reliability, last seen) is its own state, in its own table (§4).
78: - Treats payloads as opaque beyond their routing header. Orchestrator values such as a `RoomId` may pass through
79:   it (a typing indicator's room, the frontiers in a ping): it **carries them, never interprets them**. It never
80:   branches on a room, never looks at the DAG or membership, and never decides what content to send. When it needs
81:   content it does not own (the frontiers it
82:   advertises in a ping), it asks through an interface it declares itself, implemented by the orchestrator.
83: - Folds transport health into its own `LocalLinkStatus` (`Router.localLinkStatus`); transport types stop at the
84:   router.
85: 
86: ### Transports — "move these bytes"
87: 
88: - Speak **remotes and bytes**: a session key (`PeerId` for WebRTC, `TorEndpoint` for Tor) and `BinaryEnvelope`
89:   frames.
90: - Implement `SessionTransport<K>`: per-remote session states, idempotent open/close, send on an open session.
91: - Know nothing about the database, accounts, identity, crypto sessions or retry policy. The only key a transport
92:   holds is its own (the onion key, kept in Tor's state directory).
93: - Details: [`transport.md`](transport.md).
94: 
95: ### Services beside the layers
96: 
97: - **protocol** — wire types and codecs (`BinaryEnvelope`, `MessageEnvelope`, `SystemEnvelope`,
98:   `BootstrapEnvelope`, `FileEnvelope`, `WebRtcSignalEnvelope`), ids (`AccountId`, `PeerId`, `RoomId`,
99:   `TorEndpoint`), and the observability profiles (`EnvelopeObservability`) that say which routing metadata is
100:   visible on the wire. Also the public identity vocabulary that travels on the wire (`protocol/identity`: public
101:   keys, prekey ids, `SignedPreKey`, `AccountIdentity`, `DeviceIdentity`) and the WebRTC signal types. It is the
102:   bottom of the graph: it depends on nothing else in the core. Codecs encode and decode; signing, hashing and
103:   encryption happen elsewhere (e.g. room ids are hashed by the DAG's `RoomIds` from bytes `protocol` defines).
104: - **crypto** — primitives (`CryptoProvider`), private keys (`crypto/keys`), identity services, signatures, and 1:1
105:   E2EE (X3DH, Double Ratchet, session manager). The identity services: `LocalIdentity` (who this device is;
106:   readable by every layer), `LocalKeys` (this device's private keys; crypto, protection and setup only) and
107:   `PeerKeys` (peers' public keys, strictly resolved). Owns its stores, including the keyring-backed key store.
108: - **protection** — turns a payload into protected envelope bytes and back (sign, encrypt, verify, decrypt) for
109:   each envelope family. Used by the router; built on crypto.
110: - **persistence** — the database only: SQLDelight schema (`.sq`), migrations (`.sqm`), driver and column
111:   adapters, and the generated queries. It is infrastructure, not a layer. Stores — interface and SQL
112:   implementation — live with the layer that owns their tables: `crypto/store`, `routing/store`,
113:   `orchestrator/store`, `orchestrator/identity` (§4). So do the types a column maps to (`OpkStatus` in
114:   `crypto/store`, `VerificationState` in `orchestrator/dag`); the schema may name them, hand-written
115:   persistence code does not.
116: - **config** — each layer defines its own config type next to its code (`OrchestratorConfig`, `RouterConfig`,
117:   `TorBackendConfig`, …). `config` itself holds only layer-free types: the GUI's setting model (`Setting`,
118:   `ConfigValue`, `UpdateResult`) and the config-file watcher. The aggregate of all layer configs (`RuntimeConfig`), the
119:   settings registry that maps file keys onto it, and loading, watching and distributing
120:   config live in the composition root.
121: - **Size limits** — each layer states only its own framing overhead (`MessageEnvelope.maxPayloadBytes`,
122:   `CryptoLimits.forSessionWireFrameBudget`); the composition root chains them from the transport limits
123:   (`wiring/MessageLimits`) and hands each consumer its piece: the router `TransportLimits`, crypto
124:   `CryptoLimits`, the orchestrator the max text size.
125: - **logging** — `AppLog`, usable everywhere.
126: 
127: ## 3. Dependency rules
128: 
129: A package may import only what its row allows (plus `logging`, `config`, `persistence` and the standard
130: libraries).
131: 
132: | Package      | May depend on                                                                   |
133: |--------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
134: | protocol     | —                                                                               |
135: | transport    | protocol                                                                        |
136: | crypto       | protocol                                                                        |
137: | protection   | crypto, protocol                                                                |
138: | routing      | transport, protection, protocol, crypto's identity views (`crypto.identity`)    |
139: | orchestrator | routing (`Router`, its vocabulary, and the ports it declares), crypto, protocol |
140: | config       | protocol                                                                        |
141: | persistence  | protocol                                                                        |
142: | wiring       | everything                                                                      |
143: 
144: `config` and `persistence` are importable from every layer, so they never import a layer back (only
145: `protocol` and `logging`); otherwise they would be a back door around the table.
146: 
147: Consequences:
148: 
149: - When a lower layer needs something from a higher one, it **declares an interface in its own package** and the
150:   higher layer implements it. The composition root connects them. Lower layers never import upper-layer types.
151: - Exceptions cross a layer boundary only as the receiving layer's own vocabulary (e.g. a crypto failure becomes a
152:   protection verdict before the router sees it).
153: - The rules are checked by `ArchitectureTest` (jvmTest); a new dependency that breaks the table fails the build.
154:   Violations still being worked off are listed there by file as known debt — the list only shrinks.
155: 
156: ## 4. Data ownership
157: 
158: Every table has exactly **one owning layer**, and only that layer writes it. Other layers read through narrow
159: read-only interfaces that the *reading* layer declares (the router's `DeviceDirectory`, crypto's
160: `PeerKeyDirectory`). A store with write methods is handed only to the component that is allowed to write.
161: 
162: | Tables                                                               | Owner          | Writers                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
163: |----------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
164: | `accounts`, `devices`, `signed_prekeys`                              | orchestrator   | the global fold (`IdentityWriter`); intro seeding of provisional rows (`ProvisionalIdentitySeeder`, onboarding only); this device's own rows and prekeys at setup (`LocalIdentityStore`, identity provisioning) |
165: | `one_time_prekeys`, `crypto_sessions`, `crypto_session_skipped_keys` | crypto         | the session manager and its key services                                                                                                                                                                        |
166: | `messages`, `message_parents`, `causal_hold`                         | orchestrator   | the DAG engine                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
167: | `message_deliveries`                                                 | orchestrator   | the delivery tracker                                                                                                                                                                                            |
168: | `rooms`, `room_members`                                              | orchestrator   | the room fold; GLOBAL membership: the global fold (the GLOBAL room itself is seeded by the schema)                                                                                                              |
169: | `pending_syncs`, `pending_sync_candidate_accounts`                   | orchestrator   | the sync coordinator                                                                                                                                                                                            |
170: | `sync_attempts`, `sync_declined_devices`                             | routing        | the sync retry processor                                                                                                                                                                                        |
171: | `device_routes`                                                      | routing        | the router: endpoints it proved, reliability, last seen (a proven endpoint overrides the declared one in `devices`)                                                                                             |
172: | `outbox`, `dedup`                                                    | routing        | the router                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
173: | `file_transfers`, `file_chunk_tracker`, `spaces`                     | not in use yet | —                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
174: 
175: Rules:
176: 
177: - The folds are the only writers of state derived from the event chains. Services that act on the user's behalf (add a
178:   member, remove a device) **publish an event**; they never write the projected tables directly.
179: - What the router learns about reaching a device (proven endpoint, availability, last seen) is never part of the
180:   orchestrator's identity model. The router reports it only per account (`onlineAccounts`, `Router.accountReach()`),
181:   never per device. The endpoint a device declared on the chain is identity data and stays with the orchestrator.
182: - The full identity store (`IdentityStore`) is held only by the composition root. Everyone else gets the view
183:   they need: `IdentityReader`, `IdentityWriter`, `ProvisionalIdentitySeeder`, `LocalIdentityStore`,
184:   `PeerKeyDirectory`, `DeviceDirectory`.
185: - Each `.sq` file's generated `*Queries` is used only in its owner's package; `ArchitectureTest` checks it.
186:   Adding a table means adding a row here and an owner there in the same change.
187: - Schema changes ship with a migration; the database is the only thing that has to survive a rewrite.
188:   Migrations run with foreign keys off and are checked with `foreign_key_check` before they come back on, so a
189:   table can be rebuilt in place (SQLite's procedure for changes `ALTER TABLE` can't make).
190: 
191: ### Data types
192: 
193: - **Keys are typed.** Public keys (`SigningPublicKey`, `EncryptionPublicKey`, under `PublicKey` in
194:   `protocol/identity`) and private keys (`SigningPrivateKey`, `EncryptionPrivateKey`, under `PrivateKey` in
195:   `crypto/keys`) are separate hierarchies, so a private key can never stand where a wire key is expected. All
196:   wrap the bytes, compare by content, and never print a private key. Prekey ids are `SignedPreKeyId` /
197:   `OneTimePreKeyId`. Raw `ByteArray` keys appear only at the wire (codecs, payload classes)
198:   and inside the ratchet; convert at that boundary.
199: - **Keyring entries are `KeySlot`s.** Each key the app holds outside the database has one slot; its keyring
200:   name never changes for an existing slot.
201: - **One entity per table, named for what it is.** `Account` (with its `AccountDevice`s, in
202:   `orchestrator/identity`) is the stored account; `AccountIdentity`/`DeviceIdentity` are what an account or
203:   device presents about itself (carried in bootstrap payloads), and a stored entity contains its identity rather
204:   than duplicating it. Public and private halves are separate types:
205:   `SignedPreKey` is what peers see, `LocalSignedPreKey` adds our private half. No `Row`/`Record` suffixes.
206: - **Generated SQLDelight classes never leave their store.** Column adapters map columns straight to these
207:   types where they can.
208: 
209: ## 5. The composition root
210: 
211: The composition root (`wiring`) builds the core in two phases, each built fresh on every start:
212: 
213: - **Vault** (`VaultGraph`): what exists as soon as the data directory is open, before any local identity —
214:   config store, key store, database, the identity store with `LocalIdentity`, `LocalKeys` and `PeerKeys`,
215:   provisioning. Boot diagnosis and the
216:   first half of setup run against it.
217: - **Node** (`NodeGraph`): everything that needs the local identity — stores, crypto sessions, protection,
218:   transports, the router, the DAG, the folds, sync, onboarding and the runtime services. Its constructor only
219:   wires; `start()` starts the parts in dependency order.
220: 
221: The orchestrator never constructs anything. It declares what its lifecycle needs (`NodeAssembler`, `Vault`,
222: `Node` in `orchestrator/boot`), and `wiring` implements those. The public entry point
223: `OrchestratorFactory` lives in `wiring`; each platform (JVM, Android, iOS) gives it a `Platform` (keyring,
224: database driver, Tor and WebRTC backends, logger, config watcher).
225: 
226: - `DefaultOrchestrator` is the lifecycle only: lock, boot diagnosis, setup, start/stop, reset, and the
227:   public state flows.
228: - Setup is split around node assembly: `LocalSetupPreparer` provisions the identity on the vault, and
229:   `LocalSetup` finishes the chosen path on the running node (`orchestrator/onboarding`).
230: - **Components subscribe to their own inputs.** A component that reacts to another's flow takes that flow (or
231:   its owner) in its constructor and collects it in its own `start()`. The composition root contains no
232:   `launch`/`collect`; the only collectors in the lifecycle mirror the node's flows into the stable public ones.
233: - Each component takes its dependencies through its constructor as interfaces; no service locators, no
234:   `lateinit` wiring after construction. Something that needs a value only known at runtime (the local device
235:   id) is built after that value is resolved, not patched in later.
236: 
237: ## 6. Delivery model
238: 
239: Effectively-once delivery rests on the **pull path**, not the push path. Every sent message is appended to the
240: local DAG first; pings advertise DAG tips (frontiers); peers pull what they miss with sync requests. The outbox
241: push (dispatch + ACK/NACK retry) is a latency optimization — a deferred or expired push is a latency problem,
242: never a loss.
243: 
244: - Sync is split along the same line as everything else. The orchestrator owns **what** is missing, which
245:   accounts may hold it, and what may be served to whom (`pending_syncs`, the serve gate). The router owns **asking**:
246:   which candidate device, when, and carrying the request and reply. It reads the content through
247:   `SyncPayloadProvider`, an interface it declares and the orchestrator implements, and the orchestrator hands
248:   it each sync with `Router.startSync`. Only candidate devices with an open link are asked; with none, their
249:   links are nudged and the sync is asked the moment one comes up. Each attempt is one sync request sent
250:   through the outbox with a short lifetime (`syncAttemptTimeout`). A `DECLINED` NACK rules that device out for
251:   the sync; expiry or any other NACK only moves it behind the other candidates, and the next one is asked at
252:   once. An ACK leaves the backoff to schedule the next attempt. A sync ends only when its pending sync does.
253: - The router owns pings as a mechanism (liveness, link adoption, availability). The frontiers inside a ping
254:   come from the orchestrator (`FrontierSnapshotProvider`, per account), and received frontiers go back to it
255:   per account; what they mean (new syncs, reopening declined ones, re-pushing a removal) is decided there.
256: - A frontier can name a room this device has never seen (e.g. a device just added to an account that is already
257:   in rooms): the room gets a provisional `UNKNOWN` row, as on ingest, so a sync row can be created, and the
258:   room's own history fills it in.
259: - Sync rows die when their target arrives in any state (`Inserted` or `BecameOrphan`): an arrived orphan's fetch
260:   is satisfied and its missing parents get fresh rows. This keeps out-of-order delivery (normal for
261:   store-and-forward) from leaking sync rows.
262: - Repair that follows from content (e.g. re-delivering a removal node to a device whose ping shows it never saw
263:   its removal) is decided by the orchestrator and sent through the router as an ordinary payload.
264: 
265: ### Outcomes and delivery state
266: 
267: - Every outbox entry that someone waits on carries a tag saying what it is for (a message push, a bootstrap
268:   packet, a sync attempt). However the entry leaves the outbox — ACK, terminal NACK, expiry — the outcome is
269:   reported once, by tag, to whoever waits on it. New outbox traffic that needs its outcome gets a tag; it
270:   does not add another callback path.
271: - Upward, the router reports only push-path ACKs, per account (`Router.deliveries`). An ACK proves delivery;
272:   its absence proves nothing, since relays and the pull path never ACK to the original sender.
273: - What the user sees is the orchestrator's: the delivery tracker records an account as holding a message on
274:   a push ACK, or when that account's ping frontier descends from the message (which covers relay and sync
275:   delivery). There is no "failed" state while the pull path exists — only "not known delivered yet".
276: 
277: ### Protection verdicts
278: 
279: `ProtectionDisposition` is two-valued:
280: 
281: - `PERMANENT` — these bytes are dead (bad signature, replay, violation, corrupt).
282: - `DEFER` — prerequisites missing (session/identity not ready). There is no "retryable" protection verdict:
283:   retry policy is owned by the outbox.
284: 
285: ### Inbound and outbound dispositions
286: 
287: - `DEFER` is silent by design: no ACK, no NACK, dedup row cleared, so the sender's resend is processed fresh
288:   once the prerequisite lands. A NACK here would either replay a stale verdict for later duplicates or falsely
289:   ACK the packet through the duplicate-replay path.
290: - `ACK` means processed — never sent before a successful decrypt-and-handle.
291: - The sender owns a message until it decrypts on the receiver: there is no inbound hold queue; the sender's
292:   outbox retry is the only recovery path for undecryptable packets.
293: - A received NACK's meaning is a pure function of its reason, decided in one place in the router. Terminal
294:   reasons (`PERMANENT_PROTECTION_FAILED`, `DECODE_FAILED`, `UNSUPPORTED_TYPE`, `EXPIRED`, `DECLINED`) delete
295:   the outbox row; `WRONG_TARGET` keeps it (endpoint reconciliation self-heals). An unrecognized reason never
296:   deletes — never act destructively on confusion with a newer peer.
297: - Outbound `DEFER` (session not ready at protect time) surfaces as a deferred device count in the router's
298:   account report. The message stays in the DAG and delivery falls back to the pull path; the orchestrator shows
299:   that member as pending, never as failed. There is deliberately no staging table: epoch-1 encryption
300:   self-bootstraps, so the remaining defer windows are round-trip-scale races the pull path covers.
301: - The outbox has no processing round: each due entry is claimed (attempt and next retry recorded first) and sent
302:   on its own, so a slow send never delays what is queued behind it. In-flight sends are capped globally and per
303:   target. Sends never open a connection: an entry whose peer has no open link waits for one. Bootstrap packets
304:   with an explicit endpoint are the exception: Tor dials a stream for them on demand.
305: - Unknown devices: an ACK/NACK from a device with no row is accepted only when it refers to a bootstrap packet
306:   in our outbox addressed to exactly that device (a recovering device can't verify its sponsor's signature yet;
307:   the unguessable packet id authenticates the reply). It is never answered. Accepted bootstrap ACKs are
308:   reported to the orchestrator so onboarding can show "request delivered".
309: 
310: ## 7. Identity and keys
311: 
312: - Identity lives in the global chain: accounts and devices, each with signing and encryption keys. The global
313:   fold projects it into `accounts`/`devices`.
314: - The account signing key exists only on the account's first device (genesis, new account, or recovery-key
315:   import). A device added to an existing account never holds it: it starts on a key-less stand-in local account,
316:   and when the fold confirms the device under its real account, that account becomes the local one (the
317:   stand-in and its memberships fold into it).
318: - Device identity keys are immutable; there is no identity-key rotation.
319: - Private keys are reached only through `LocalKeys`; peers' public keys through `PeerKeys`, which throws on a
320:   missing record rather than returning a partial one.
321: - Private keys and the database master key live in the OS keyring, outside the data directory. Deleting the data
322:   directory therefore leaves keys behind; a freshly created database can't own any of them, so boot deletes
323:   them and goes to setup. A reset deletes everything in the data directory except the held `app.lock`.
324: - The database is encrypted with the keyring-held master key.
325: - E2EE design, conscious trade-offs and the open backlog: [`e2ee.md`](e2ee.md).
326: 
327: ## 8. Feature status
328: 
329: Working:
330: 
331: - Tor transport with long-lived streams, self-recovery and reachability checks; WebRTC data channels with
332:   signaling over Tor.
333: - Router: outbox with retries, relays/store-and-forward, ACK/NACK, dedup, link keeping, pings, availability.
334: - 1:1 E2EE (X3DH + Double Ratchet) for messages and WebRTC signaling.
335: - Global chain (accounts, devices, admin roles), rooms with a membership fold, the message DAG and sync.
336: - Onboarding by invite, adding devices, recovery.
337: - Compose desktop GUI.
338: 
339: Not done yet:
340: 
341: - File transfer (envelope family exists; protection, pipeline and storage are not built — the agreed design is
342:   in [`file/design.md`](file/design.md)).
343: - Audio/video media (session contracts exist; media tracks do not).
344: - Mobile: push and background behavior, network monitoring on Android/iOS.
345: - Signed-prekey rotation and the remaining epoch lifecycle work (see [`e2ee.md`](e2ee.md)).
346: - Metadata minimization beyond the current observability profiles (desirable, not a v1 blocker).
347: 
348: ## 9. Writing new code
349: 
350: 1. **Pick the layer by vocabulary.** If the code talks about rooms, members, messages or accounts, it is
351:    orchestrator code. If it talks about devices, envelopes, retries or links, it is router code. If it only
352:    moves bytes, it is transport code.
353: 2. **Check the dependency table.** If you need something from a higher layer, declare an interface in your own
354:    package and let the higher layer implement it.
355: 3. **Check data ownership.** Write only tables your layer owns; read others through a read-only view your
356:    layer declares. If identity or room state must change, publish an event and let the fold write it.
357:    Use the typed keys, ids and entities (§4, data types), not raw bytes and strings.
358: 4. **Wire it in the composition root**, with constructor-injected interfaces.
359: 5. **Wire types go in `protocol`.** A new envelope or payload gets a codec with round-trip tests and an
360:    observability profile if it adds routing metadata.
361: 6. **Respect the delivery contract** (§6): never ACK before handling, never NACK a `DEFER`, never delete on an
362:    unknown reason.
363: 7. **Keep the docs honest.** A change that moves a rule in this guide updates the guide in the same change;
364:    mechanism details go in the layer's own doc.

1: # Transport & links
2: 
3: How devices hold connections to each other and how bytes cross Tor and WebRTC. The layer rules (what the transport may
4: and may not know) are in [`guide.md`](guide.md); this file covers how it works.
5: 
6: ## Sessions (links)
7: 
8: Tor delivers over long-lived streams, not one connection per packet. Tor runs many streams concurrently, but
9: setting one up to an onion takes seconds, and to an offline peer it can hang for minutes. So connections are
10: kept open in the background, and sends only use connections that are already open.
11: 
12: - Both session transports implement one contract (`SessionTransport<K>` in `transport/session`): per-remote
13:   `sessionStates` where `CONNECTED` holds iff `hasSession`, plus idempotent, asynchronous
14:   `openSession`/`closeSession`. WebRTC keys sessions by device id, Tor by onion endpoint.
15: - The router sees them per device through `PeerLinks` (`routing/link`). Transport choice (`OutboundPolicy`)
16:   takes the most preferred open link (`RouterConfig.linkPreference`: WebRTC, then Tor). With no link, outbox
17:   entries wait (deferred without counting an attempt) and relay deposits plus the pull path cover delivery;
18:   system traffic has Tor dial a stream on demand. Any link coming up wakes the peer's outbox entries.
19: - Relays (store-and-forward copies of a message, so delivery doesn't need sender and recipient online at the
20:   same time) are used only when the direct path looks doubtful: no open link when the message is sent or when
21:   it comes due, no ACK within `relayBackupAfter` of a send over a link, or a retry. Each outbox entry records
22:   its backup state (`relay_backup`), so copies are made at most once, across restarts too. While a link
23:   delivers, relays carry nothing.
24: - `LinkKeeper` keeps links open to a target set over any session transport, with per-peer exponential
25:   backoff, capped concurrent opens, prompt reopen when a link drops, and a readiness gate. The router runs one
26:   for Tor (all active peers, gated on `TorHealth.Ready`). WebRTC sessions stay on-demand (`ProactiveSessionOpener`).
27: - Pings go only to linked peers. A successful link open pings the peer, which exchanges frontiers on connect.
28:   A failed open counts as an unanswered probe for availability scoring.
29: 
30: ## Tor
31: 
32: ### Wire
33: 
34: - A connection starts with a magic int. Every connection we dial to a peer is a stream (`TOR_STREAM_MAGIC`):
35:   a hello naming the dialer's endpoint, then records (`ACCEPT`, `DATA`, `KEEPALIVE`; unknown types are
36:   skipped). The self-reachability probe (`TOR_PROBE_MAGIC`) is a connection to our own onion whose nonce our
37:   listener echoes back. One-shot frames (`TOR_TRANSPORT_FRAME_MAGIC`: one frame, then close) are no longer
38:   sent but still accepted from older builds; receiving them can be dropped once no such builds remain. Older
39:   builds can't accept streams, so to them mixed-version devices rely on relays and the pull path.
40: 
41: ### Streams
42: 
43: - A send with no session dials a stream on demand (bootstrap targets, system traffic to an unlinked peer).
44:   Streams nobody asked to keep — dialed on demand, or inbound and not adopted — are transient: they close after
45:   `transientLinkIdleTimeout` without envelopes. Unadopted inbound streams have their own cap (`maxUnadoptedInbound`).
46: - A stream we dialed is a session once the far end's app sends `ACCEPT`. A stream someone else dialed only
47:   carries replies (ACK/NACK go back on the stream the packet arrived on) until the router adopts it. It adopts
48:   a stream once an authenticated ping from the claimed device arrives on it: pings are never relayed, so this
49:   proves who dialed. When both sides dial each other, the side with the higher onion closes its own dialed
50:   stream after adopting the other.
51: - Idle streams exchange keepalives, and a stream with nothing received for `sessionIdleTimeout` is closed:
52:   Tor gives no timely signal when the far end disappears. A stream carrying our envelopes is held to the much
53:   shorter `sessionResponseTimeout`: each burst of envelopes ends with an `ECHO` record the far end answers at
54:   once, so a peer that vanished is noticed within seconds of sending to it.
55: 
56: ### Backend lifecycle and health
57: 
58: - `TorBackend.start()` returns once the daemon's SOCKS listener is up and the onion is added; it does not wait
59:   for bootstrap. Bootstrap progress, Tor's own stall reason (`STATUS_CLIENT` `REASON`/`HOSTADDR`) and network
60:   liveness are reported through `TorBackend.health` (`TorHealth`). Callers must not dial an onion (including
61:   their own) before it is published: Tor caches a failed descriptor lookup and holds or refuses the stream for
62:   minutes. kmp-tor returns the same runtime per data directory for the life of the process, so observers bound
63:   to a backend instance are subscribed in `start()` and removed in `stop()`, never registered in the builder.
64: - Network changes (desktop: `JvmNetworkMonitor`, which polls interfaces and detects sleep from wall-clock gaps;
65:   Android/iOS: none yet) reach Tor two ways. Online/offline goes through kmp-tor's `NetworkObserver`
66:   (`TorNetworkObserver`, process-wide) as `DisableNetwork`. A switch or wake-up keeps the device online, so
67:   `KmpTorBackend` cycles `DisableNetwork` itself, drops cached onion lookups and re-verifies publication.
68:   Setting `DisableNetwork` closes Tor's SOCKS listener and re-enabling reopens it on a new port; the backend
69:   re-reads the port (`GETINFO net/listeners/socks`) when a local SOCKS connect fails.
70: - Status path to the GUI: `TorHealth` (incl. `NoNetwork` from the monitor), `TorPublishState` and the current
71:   `TorRecoveryStep` go from the transport to the router, which folds them into one `Router.localLinkStatus`
72:   (`LocalLinkStatus`, in `routing/router/LocalLinkStatus.kt`: precedence, recovery steps, and which bootstrap
73:   `REASON` codes mean "relays unreachable"). The orchestrator maps that state for state to the public
74:   `LocalTransportStatus`. Tor types stop at the router. Tor's stall reason travels as problem detail, never as
75:   headline.
76: 
77: ### Recovery
78: 
79: - `TorSupervisor` (inside `KmpTorBackend`) recovers a Tor that is stuck while the network is fine: no bootstrap
80:   progress for `bootstrapStallTimeout` (2 min; Tor can stall silently and also recovers from many stalls on its
81:   own), or publication DEGRADED. It escalates one `TorRecoveryStep` per incident — cycle DisableNetwork, restart
82:   the daemon, restart with a purged directory cache (`tor/cache/cached-*`), restart with reset guard state
83:   (`tor/work/data/state`, at most once per `guardResetMinInterval`, recorded in `tor/guard_reset_at`) — and
84:   starts over once Tor is up and published. Past the ladder it keeps restarting with a backed-off stall
85:   timeout. While healthy it silently re-proves reachability every `reachabilityRecheckInterval`. No step
86:   touches the onion key. The current step reaches the GUI as `LocalTransportStatus.Recovering`.
87: - Stale onion lookups: Tor remembers "descriptor not found" for minutes, and a directory relay that never
88:   answers holds a stream for Tor's full two-minute SOCKS timeout. The backend tracks unanswered `HS_DESC`
89:   fetches per onion (`DescriptorFetchTracker`) and ends a send attempt or self-probe stuck on one for
90:   `descriptorFetchStallTimeout` (20 s). SOCKS code 4 surfaces as `TorException.OnionNotFound`. When a Tor link
91:   open fails this way for a peer the availability registry says is online, the router asks
92:   `TorTransport.refreshOnionLookups()` to drop the cached miss and retries after `onionRefreshRetryDelay`.
93:   NEWNYM is global (it also discards warm circuits to every other peer), so refreshes requested from outside
94:   the backend's own recovery are throttled (`onionLookupRefreshMinInterval`, 30 s).
95: 
96: ## WebRTC
97: 
98: - `JvmWebRtcBackend` uses webrtc-java for offer/answer/ICE and data channels.
99: - Signaling goes over Tor: the transport emits outgoing signals and accepts incoming ones; the router
100:   protects them and carries them as envelopes. The WebRTC transport never talks to Tor itself.
101: - Session state contract: the shared `SessionTransport` one (`CONNECTED` iff the envelope data channel is
102:   open); the backend is the single writer of state, so subscribers may treat replayed states as ground truth.
103:   `ProactiveSessionOpener.awaitSession` is event-driven on this stream (with a slow re-open safety net for
104:   silently lost signaling).
105: - AV session contracts (request/accept/reject/state/control) exist at the transport API; media-track handling
106:   in the backend is not complete.
107: 
108: ## Testing
109: 
110: - Integration tests include a live loopback Tor test, a local two-peer WebRTC test and a live Tor + WebRTC
111:   test (opt-in via `-PintegrationTests=true`).
112: - Some live/native WebRTC tests can be flaky with thread-attach warnings from webrtc-java.
